questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: Explain the meaning of robotics.
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a robot and robotics. Use the words machine and study in your answer.
questions.answer: A robot is a machine used to carry out tasks under instructions or control. Robotics is the study of robots, including how they are designed, built and used.
questions.explanation: The terms refer to an object and a field of study rather than two different machines.

markingGuide.description: Describes a robot as a task-performing machine.
Describes robotics as the study of robots.

questions.deliveryNote: Written concept or recognition preparation only. This task does not establish physical component identification, assembly, wiring or robot programming. No equipment is to be powered or handled for this question.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: Explain the meaning of robotics.
questions.prompt: A pupil says a machine can only be a robot if it has a human-shaped head and hands. Give a different possible shape of a robot and explain why human appearance is not the deciding feature.
questions.answer: A robot might be a wheeled machine or a mechanical arm. What matters is its ability to carry out a task under instructions or control, not whether it looks human.
questions.explanation: Accept other suitable non-humanoid examples. Do not imply every machine is a robot simply because it has wheels.

markingGuide.description: Gives a suitable non-human-shaped robot example.
Explains that task performance under instructions or control matters more than human appearance.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: List basic types of robots.
questions.prompt: Two robots both have wheels. One carries materials around a factory; the other is a play robot used for simple games. Why should their purpose be considered when deciding their type?
questions.answer: A robot's type can depend on the work it is designed to do. Wheels describe how it moves, while factory work and play describe different purposes.
questions.explanation: A shared physical feature does not mean the robots have the same application category.

markingGuide.description: Links classification to purpose or work.
Distinguishes wheel-based movement from factory/play purpose.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: Explain basic features of robots.
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a sensor and an actuator in a robot. Give one example of information a sensor could obtain and one physical action an actuator could produce.
questions.answer: A sensor obtains information, such as light level or whether a switch is pressed. An actuator produces a physical action, such as turning a wheel or opening a gripper.
questions.explanation: Accept other suitable sensing and action examples without requiring the same robot model.

markingGuide.description: Explains sensing and gives a suitable information example.
Explains actuation and gives a suitable action example.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: Explain basic features of robots.
questions.prompt: A pupil thinks every robot sensor must take photographs. Explain why a touch sensor or a temperature sensor shows that this is wrong.
questions.answer: A touch sensor can detect contact, and a temperature sensor can measure how warm or cold something is. Neither needs to take a photograph to provide information.
questions.explanation: Sensors can collect different kinds of information. A camera is one possible sensor, not the definition of all sensors.

markingGuide.description: Gives a correct non-photographic sensing function.
Explains that obtaining information does not always require a camera.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: Explain basic features of robots.
questions.prompt: A robot arm stays fixed to a table while its gripper opens and closes. Does remaining in one place mean it has no actuator? Explain.
questions.answer: No. An actuator can open and close the gripper even when the whole robot does not travel across the floor.
questions.explanation: Physical action can occur in one part of a robot; locomotion of the whole robot is not required.

markingGuide.description: Recognises that the robot can still have an actuator.
Links the actuator to gripper movement.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: Explain benefits and uses of robots.
questions.prompt: A remotely operated robot can take measurements near a damaged structure while its operator stays farther away. Explain one safety benefit of this use, without claiming that the robot makes the entire situation risk-free.
questions.answer: It can reduce the need for a person to enter the hazardous area directly. The site still requires proper controls and checking; the robot does not remove every danger.
questions.explanation: The example concerns a general safety benefit, not instructions to approach a damaged structure.

markingGuide.description: Explains reduced human exposure to the hazardous area.
Recognises that other risks or controls remain.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: Explain benefits and uses of robots.
questions.prompt: A family enjoys a toy robot that responds to simple programmed movements during a game. Explain how this illustrates recreation as a benefit of robotics.
questions.answer: The robot provides enjoyment through play and interaction. A robot does not need to perform factory work to have a useful recreational purpose.
questions.explanation: The example is fictional and does not recommend a particular product or suggest unsupervised equipment use.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: Explain benefits and uses of robots.
questions.prompt: A hospital uses a delivery robot to take meal trays along an approved route. Explain the service it provides and one way this could help staff use their time.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: State functions of basic components in a robot.
questions.prompt: A pupil says a microcontroller can carry out any new task without being given instructions. Explain what role its program has in controlling a robot.
questions.answer: The program supplies the instructions and rules that the microcontroller executes. The robot's behaviour depends on that program and the information it receives.
questions.explanation: Calling a controller a brain is an analogy; it does not mean the component automatically knows every desired task.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the program as executable instructions or rules.
Connects those instructions with the robot's behaviour.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: State functions of basic components in a robot.
questions.prompt: A model robot has a small LED used to show that it is ready. Explain why the LED cannot take the place of the motor that turns a wheel.
questions.answer: The LED produces light as an indicator. A motor produces movement, so the two parts perform different output functions.
questions.explanation: An indicator and a motion-producing component are not interchangeable just because both are controlled outputs.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the LED's light output.
Identifies the motor's motion-producing function.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: State functions of basic components in a robot.
questions.prompt: A robot model has a tactile switch labelled Start. Explain what pressing the switch supplies to the control system and why the label alone does not make the robot start.
questions.answer: Pressing it supplies an input, such as a change in the switch state. The program must interpret that input and command the required start behaviour.
questions.explanation: A physical input is not the complete programmed response.

markingGuide.description: Identifies switch press as an input.
Explains the need for programmed interpretation or response.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: State functions of basic components in a robot.
questions.prompt: Why can a group of LEDs arranged as a display show a simple arrow more clearly than one small indicator LED?
questions.answer: Different LEDs in the group can be lit in a pattern that outlines an arrow. One indicator mainly signals through its light state and cannot by itself form that multi-point shape.
questions.explanation: The answer concerns the display's arranged light points. No particular display size or wiring arrangement is assumed.

markingGuide.description: Links multiple controllable light points with a pattern.
Explains the limitation of one indicator for making the arrow shape.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: Explain the functions of breadboard, resistor and jumper wire.
questions.prompt: A teacher plans to try several different arrangements of components before choosing a final circuit design. Explain one reason a solderless breadboard is useful for this purpose.
questions.answer: Components can be inserted into its contacts and rearranged without soldering, making temporary circuit arrangements easier to change.
questions.explanation: This is written preparation only. It does not ask the pupil to build, connect or energise a circuit.

markingGuide.description: Identifies temporary connections without soldering.
Explains that components can be rearranged during prototyping.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: Explain the functions of breadboard, resistor and jumper wire.
questions.prompt: Explain the function of a jumper wire in a classroom circuit model. Does a wire itself store the robot's program?
questions.answer: A jumper wire makes an electrical connection between circuit points or components. It does not store the robot's program; program storage and execution belong to the control electronics.
questions.explanation: The explanation distinguishes an electrical connection from computation.

markingGuide.description: Describes making an electrical connection.
Rejects the wire as the program-storage component.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: Explain the functions of breadboard, resistor and jumper wire.
questions.prompt: A teacher's simple LED-circuit diagram includes a resistor chosen for that circuit. Explain its current-limiting purpose and why it should not simply be replaced by a plain connecting wire.
questions.answer: The resistor opposes current flow and helps limit the current through the LED. Replacing it with a plain connection removes that intended current-limiting function.
questions.explanation: No resistor value, circuit assembly or power test is requested. Component selection requires the actual circuit specifications.

markingGuide.description: Explains resistance or current limitation.
Explains loss of the intended limiting function with a plain connection.
